claims.text: SPS at 1800–2000 °C under controlled uniaxial pressure will lower the preparation temperature required for single-phase ZrB2.
SPS at 1800–2000 °C will produce near-fully-dense ZrB2.
The SPS-produced ZrB2 will have minimized porosity.
Reduced porosity will enhance resistance to hole formation and failure during prolonged liquid-plating exposure.
The proposed intervention uses rapid pulsed electric currents and uniaxial pressure.
The proposed SPS preparation window is 1800–2000 °C, 50–100 MPa, and a 5–10 minute dwell in an inert atmosphere.
Pulsed heating and applied pressure cause rapid densification of ZrB2.
Rapid SPS densification produces a fine microstructure with significantly reduced residual porosity.
Pulsed currents and pressure accelerate diffusion and particle rearrangement in ZrB2.
Accelerated diffusion and particle rearrangement promote pore closure.
Short SPS processing minimizes high-temperature exposure and thereby limits grain growth and interconnected microstructural defects.
Eliminating interconnected microstructural defects reduces pathways for liquid infiltration during plating.
SPS-processed ZrB2 will have comparable or superior density relative to conventionally sintered ZrB2.
SPS-processed ZrB2 will have comparable or superior mechanical resilience relative to conventionally sintered ZrB2.
SPS-processed ZrB2 will exhibit fewer and smaller pores than conventionally sintered ZrB2.
SPS-processed ZrB2 will exhibit reduced failure during long-duration exposure to liquid-plating baths.
Conventional ZrB2 sintering above 2300 °C typically produces greater residual porosity and more defect structures.
Residual pores and defects in conventionally sintered ZrB2 are vulnerable during extended liquid-plating exposure.
Scaling SPS to larger samples may cause nonuniform temperature distributions and microstructural inhomogeneity.

A 1000-hour controlled plating-bath comparison using identical starting powders can test whether SPS improves density, porosity, mechanical performance, and resistance to hole formation relative to conventional sintering.
